bib.title: Walking Down the Memory Maze: Beyond Context Limit through Interactive Reading

legacy_report:
SOURCE: Walking Down the Memory Maze: Beyond Context Limit through Interactive Reading (MemWalker). Howard Chen (Princeton; work done during internship at Meta AI), Ramakanth Pasunuru, Jason Weston, Asli Celikyilmaz (Meta AI). arXiv:2310.05029v1 [cs.CL], 8 Oct 2023. Preprint (no venue printed).

COVERAGE: All 15 pages, 48,564 chars, read in full (main text, limitations, references skimmed, appendix A.1/A.2 prompts and the extra trajectory). Extraction clean. Figures 2-5 are bar charts, so I got only their numbers from the extracted text.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: MemWalker builds a tree of recursive summaries (query-independent, precomputable), then the LLM navigates it by zero-shot prompting and can revert to the parent. This is hierarchical summarisation used as navigable memory, not as a replacement context.
  number: none
  setup: Stable Beluga 2 (70B LLaMA-2, 4,096-token context), no finetuning. Segments of 1000/1000/1200 tokens, max children per node 8/5/8 (QuALITY/SummScreenFD/GovReport).
  quote: "The LLM then subsequently summarizes each segment into a textual summary node. These summary nodes are progressively further summarized into higher-level summary nodes, thus building a tree structure"
  where: p.2; Sec 3 p.3; Sec 4.2 p.6

- claim: On the Long subsets, MemWalker beats every baseline (recurrence, retrieval, full-context truncation, MPT-13B 8k, LongChat-13B 16k) on all three tasks.
  number: Long accuracy 73.6 / 64.5 / 60.4 (QuALITY / SummScreenFD / GovReport)
  setup: Same Stable Beluga 2 with a 4,096 limit for all baselines. QuALITY 187 examples, SummScreenFD 306, GovReport 101. SummScreenFD and GovReport questions are LLM-generated ("who" questions from reference summaries, checked by a human). Long = over 8k / 6k / 12k tokens.
  quote: "MEMWALKER 67.4 / 73.6 67.3 / 64.5 59.4 / 60.4" (Table 2; columns Orig. / Long)
  where: Table 2, p.6

- claim: Recurrence (rolling summary carried forward) is the weakest baseline, which the authors attribute to loss of query-relevant information after several steps.
  number: Recurrence Orig./Long: 51.3/56.0, 47.7/45.4, 35.6/33.8
  setup: Segments of 2,500 tokens, summary max 500 tokens, same Stable Beluga 2.
  quote: "Recurrence 51.3 / 56.0 47.7 / 45.4 35.6 / 33.8" and "This shows the limitation of recurrence, where relevant information to the query is lost after several steps."
  where: Table 2 p.6; Sec 5 p.6; Sec 4.3 p.6

- claim: On the full (Original) datasets MemWalker does not always win. Full-context keep-right beats it on QuALITY (70.1 vs 67.4), and keep-left ties it on GovReport (59.4 vs 59.4, though keep-left drops to 56.3 on Long). The authors cite positional bias in the data. The benefit appears only when the text is much longer than the window.
  number: Orig.: keep-right 70.1 vs MemWalker 67.4 on QuALITY
  setup: Same as above. Figure 2 splits each dataset into two equal-size length buckets (0-8000 / 8000+, 0-6000 / 6000+, 0-12000 / 12000+).
  quote: "MEMWALKER is not advantageous over Full Context (with truncation left or right) baselines when the text length is short, but outperforms both types of truncation for all tasks for longer sequences."
  where: Fig 2 and text, p.7

- claim: Retrieval (Contriever) is also beaten, in particular on QuALITY.
  number: Retrieval Orig./Long on QuALITY 63.1/64.8, vs MemWalker 67.4/73.6
  setup: Contriever picks top segments to fill the 4,096 window.
  quote: "Retrieval 63.1 / 64.8 63.7 / 62.2 54.0 / 52.1"
  where: Table 2 p.6

- claim: Navigation needs a strong reasoning model. Asking for reasoning helps Stable Beluga 2 but hurts the weaker models, whose invalid-action rates are high. The authors say errors compound otherwise.
  number: Stable Beluga 2 with reasoning 67.4/67.3/59.4 vs 66.8/64.1/52.5 without. LLaMA-2-Chat 13B with reasoning 39.6/20.9/15.8 vs 48.1/25.8/21.8 without. 13B valid-action rate 73.2/75.5/69.0%.
  setup: Accuracy in Orig. setting. Reasoning ablation removes the "First provide reasoning" line from the prompt.
  quote: "Stable Beluga 2 (70B) 67.4 / 92.5 67.3 / 95.1 59.4 / 97.0 / w/o reasoning 66.8 / 100.0 64.1 / 90.5 52.5 / 98.2"
  where: Table 3, p.7

- claim: Working memory (carrying content from visited nodes into the leaf prompt) matters, so a summary-only view loses context.
  number: 5-13% accuracy drop without it. Figure 3 with vs without: 67.4 vs 62.5 (QuALITY), 67.3 vs 61.4 (SummScreenFD), 59.4 vs 46.5 (GovReport). The pairing of numbers to bars is my reading of the extracted figure text, not stated in prose.
  setup: Working memory is truncated to fit the window. The authors did not try summarising it as it grows.
  quote: "We find a significant performance degradation without working memory across all tasks, with a 5–13% drop in accuracy, showing the importance of this component."
  where: Fig 3 and text p.8; footnote p.5

- claim: The navigator recovers from wrong turns by reverting.
  number: Stray ratio 15.0 / 18.6 / 18.8%. Recovery rate 70.0 / 59.6 / 79.0%.
  setup: Stray = path containing a revert. Recovery = stray paths that end correct.
  quote: "executes a revert navigation action (and hence changes path) for around 15% − 20% of examples, but of those examples can recover and get those examples correct 70% of the time for QuALITY, ∼ 60% for SummScreenFD, and ∼ 80% for GovReport."
  where: Table 4 and text p.8

- claim: Only part of the text is read, counting tree-node summaries.
  number: 63%-69% of the text on average over all paths, 59%-64% on successful paths
  setup: Percentage of tokens processed relative to the original example, including tree-node content.
  quote: "between only 63%-69% of the text on average needs to be read to answer the question including the content of the tree nodes. Among successful paths, the reading required further reduces to 59% - 64%."
  where: Fig 4 and text p.8-9

- claim: Summarisation trade-off. Summarising larger segments and allowing more children per parent generally helps, but the gain plateaus as the children count grows. The authors state the tension as fidelity loss vs tree depth, and as flatter trees vs a harder choice at each node.
  number: none stated in prose. Fig 5 sweeps max nodes 2, 4, 8, 16 with 500- vs 1000-token segments.
  setup: QuALITY only.
  quote: "summarizing larger segments compresses more information into a node to reduce the depth of the tree, but risks losing fidelity of the content."
  where: Sec 5 p.9, Fig 5

- claim: Tree-building prompts are short and could be reused. Leaf: summarise "comprehensively into a fluent passage". Non-leaf: "Compress each summary into a much shorter summary." Concatenated child summaries are re-summarised only if they exceed the length cap.
  number: none
  setup: Appendix A.1, Table 5.
  quote: "[TEXT OF SEGMNET]. Summarize the above text comprehensively into a fluent passage." / "[SUMMARIES]. Compress each summary into a much shorter summary."
  where: Table 5, p.14

LIMITS
- The authors concede three limits. (1) Tree construction may not scale to extremely long sequences. (2) The method works only with a strong, instruction-tuned model, which they say needs to be over 70B. (3) It is zero-shot only, with no finetuning on successful paths.
- Quote: "MEMWALKER only works when the LLM exhibits a strong enough reasoning capability, which according to our experiments is required to be large (over 70B) and instruction-tuned."
- Not shown: any cost or latency figure for building the tree. Summary fidelity is not measured directly (no check of what the summaries drop). There is one model family. The test sets are small (101 to 306 examples), with no variance or confidence intervals reported. Two of the three QA sets are synthetic "who" questions.
- Dated: the base model has a 4k window, and the baselines are 2023 models. Whether the advantage holds against today's long-context models is not tested.
- Position bias is conceded as an explanation for where full-context truncation wins.

BUILDS ON
- Recurrence and summarisation carried across segments: Xu et al., 2022, which is the recurrence baseline implementation.
- Recursive tree summarisation of books: Wu et al., 2021, which did not use the tree for memory navigation.
- Retrieval: Contriever (Izacard et al., 2022), Lewis et al., 2020, Izacard & Grave, 2020, Chen et al., 2017.
- Agent-style reading: WebGPT (Nakano et al., 2021), WebShop (Yao et al., 2022), PEARL (Sun et al., 2023), Self-Notes (Lanchantin et al., 2023), Re3 (Yang et al., 2022), RecurrentGPT (Zhou et al., 2023).
- Lost-in-the-middle positional bias: Liu et al., 2023.
- Context extension: Press et al., 2022, and Chen et al., 2023 (positional interpolation).
- SCROLLS benchmark: Shaham et al., 2022.

CODE: No code. The Table 5 prompts (p.14) are the reusable artefact: construction leaf, construction non-leaf, triage and leaf. The triage prompt asks for "Reasoning: ... Action: 0 / 1 / 2" and the leaf prompt asks for "Action: -2 or -1" (-2 answers, -1 reverts). If the output cannot be parsed three times in a row, navigation ends with "no answer" (p.5).

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p.2): the two-stage procedure, a tree of summ nodes over segments, with the revert arrow. It is the quickest way to see the structure.
- Table 1 (p.4): a worked QuALITY trajectory showing revert and working memory.
- Fig 2 (p.7): accuracy by length bucket. It shows the crossover where MemWalker starts to win, once the text is much longer than the window.
- Fig 3 (p.8): working-memory ablation.
- Fig 4 (p.8): percentage of the text read.
- Fig 5 (p.9): the segment-size and children-count trade-off.
I did not run the figures script, because the captions were already in the extraction.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. Figure data came out as unlabeled number runs, so the bar-to-condition pairings for Fig 3 and Fig 4 are inferred from text order. Fig 3 is consistent with the prose ("5-13%" drop). For Fig 4 I only used the prose range. No claim here is directly about compaction of an agent's own conversation. It is about summary trees over a fixed document, so mapping it to note 05 is the caller's judgement.
